records.our_prose: A plum's worst neighbors are other Prunus you do not manage. Wild plum, chokecherry, ornamental purple-leaf plum, and abandoned plum or cherry trees are reservoirs of black knot and brown rot: the black-knot fungus overwinters in galls on those hosts and releases spores that infect your tree every wet spring, so an unmanaged thicket downwind undoes your own pruning. Where practical, remove or prune the black knot out of nearby wild hosts, or at least scout them, and site a new plum away from them.

records.our_prose: For Japanese plums, and for the many European cultivars that set more heavily with a partner, the single most useful companion is a second compatible plum. Match type to type: a Japanese cultivar needs another Japanese (or an American-Japanese hybrid) blooming at the same time, since European and Japanese plums bloom weeks apart and will not pollinate each other. Santa Rosa and Methley are widely used pollenizers for other Japanese plums; a self-fruitful European such as Stanley or Damson can stand alone but still crops more reliably with a second European nearby. Plant the pollenizer within about 100 feet so bees move freely between the trees.

records.our_prose: Hard, black, elongated warty galls have appeared along twigs and branches, girdling and killing the wood beyond them. This is black knot, the signature disease of plum, caused by the fungus Apiosporina morbosa. Growers often reach for a spray, but the galls are already established; the effective action is to cut them out. Prune each gall 3 to 4 inches below the visible swelling into clean wood during the dormant season before the fungus sporulates, remove and destroy the prunings, and deal with any wild or neglected Prunus nearby that re-infect the tree each spring.

records.our_prose: A common home-garden rate is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in spring from bloom to petal fall, up to roughly 8 to 10 cups for a mature tree. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree making 8 to 15 inches of new wood a year is fed about right, and one growing faster than that needs less nitrogen, not more.

records.our_prose: Pollination is the headline decision for plum, and it splits by type. European plums (Prunus domestica) such as Stanley, Italian prune, and damson are largely self-fruitful, so a single tree bears, though most crop somewhat more heavily with a second European variety nearby. Japanese plums (Prunus salicina) such as Santa Rosa, Burbank, and Methley are usually self-unfruitful and need a second compatible Japanese cultivar blooming at the same time; Methley and Santa Rosa are partial exceptions and also serve as good pollenizers. Crucially, European and Japanese plums bloom weeks apart and will not pollinate each other, so a pollenizer must match type. Plums are insect-pollinated, mainly by bees, so bloom-time pollinator activity matters; place a pollenizer within about 100 feet.

records.our_prose: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, with no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first so they do not stay dried out. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (that bumpy joint near the base, where the fruiting variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil you removed, water it in well, and add a stake only if the spot is windy.

records.our_prose: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two beforehand to rehydrate them. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree so the graft union (that swollen joint near the base of the trunk) sits 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line. Do not add fertilizer to the planting hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake only if the site is windy.

After the hole is backfilled, water the area well.
